text:
Chris Olave has experienced so many frightening collisions during his NFL career that fans have started joking he needs to wear multiple helmets just to make it through an entire football game. Since joining the New Orleans Saints in 2022, Olave has established himself as one of the league’s most talented young receivers through his exceptional route running, impressive hands, and ability to create separation against elite defensive backs. However, his professional career has also featured repeated concussions and dangerous collisions that have raised legitimate concerns about his long-term health. Watching a talented receiver repeatedly suffer injuries is especially frustrating because his ability to produce spectacular offensive highlights remains undeniable whenever he’s healthy.

What makes Olave’s situation particularly concerning is how seriously repeated head injuries must be treated in professional football. During the 2024 season, he suffered a concussion after a collision against the Carolina Panthers, adding to an injury history that had already interrupted his development. Although the idea of wearing multiple helmets is obviously a joke rather than a realistic medical solution, it reflects the concern fans feel whenever Olave takes another dangerous hit. His early career included consecutive 1,000-yard receiving seasons, demonstrating the extraordinary talent that made him a first-round draft selection. However, maintaining his health is far more important than any individual receiving statistic or highlight. Olave’s experiences illustrate why player safety and appropriate concussion management remain essential issues throughout professional football.

Several notable quarterbacks are dealing with injuries or facing important availability decisions heading into Week 10 of the NFL season. Patrick Mahomes, J.J. McCarthy, Deshaun Watson, Jared Goff, Gardner Minshew, Kyler Murray and Malik Willis are among the players fantasy football managers should monitor.

Wednesday's practice reports brought encouraging news for some, while other quarterbacks are facing extended absences or uncertainty surrounding their return timelines.

MORE: Top 10 NFL teams: Rankings updated after trade deadline

Patrick Mahomes, J.J. McCarthy and Deshaun Watson updates

Patrick Mahomes (knee/elbow): Mahomes was listed as a full participant on Wednesday's injury report. That's an encouraging development for the Kansas City Chiefs quarterback as he works through his knee and elbow issues. His full participation puts him in a positive position heading toward Sunday's matchup.

J.J. McCarthy (hip): McCarthy was a full participant in practice this week. The Minnesota Vikings quarterback is making progress with his hip issue, and his participation is an encouraging sign for his Week 10 availability. He is likely to start TNF against the Commanders.

Deshaun Watson (concussion): Watson will start Sunday against the Houston Texans. His expected return is a significant development for Cleveland, with the quarterback set to get back into the lineup after dealing with a concussion.

Jared Goff (chest): Goff was listed as a limited participant on Wednesday's practice report. The Detroit Lions quarterback's workload will be worth monitoring as the week progresses. It is unlikely that Goff will miss a week, though.

MORE: Bold predictions for Week 10 of 2026 NFL season

Gardner Minshew, Kyler Murray and Malik Willis injury news

Gardner Minshew (elbow): Minshew will undergo surgery and miss the remainder of the season, according to head coach Mike LaFleur. The injury ends his 2026 campaign and leaves his team without him for the rest of the year.

Kyler Murray (hamstring): Murray remains week-to-week, according to head coach Kevin O'Connell. The quarterback does not have a definitive return date, leaving his availability uncertain. It might not matter now anyway, as Kirk Cousins is expected to be the starter, and maybe even as early as this weekend.

Malik Willis (groin/core): The Miami Dolphins are placing Willis on injured reserve. The move will sideline the quarterback for at least four games, creating another significant change to Miami's quarterback situation. In a season that was already a lost one, Miami is likely going to struggle even more.

title: Inside the physical and mental toll of Malik Nabers' knee injury - ESPN
authors: Jordan Raanan, Jamison Hensley, Daniel Oyefusi, Jordan Reid, NFL Nation, Dan Graziano, Jeremy Fowler, Bill Barnwell, Courtney Cronin, Ben Baby
description:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had a conversation with his uncle before training camp in 2025.
"I kind of lost myself in the process," Nabers said while opening up about his rehab for the first time.
This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place.
Together, they monitored the wide receiver's rehab, and early on in the process, Nabers needed the mental boost.
The wide receiver is admittedly in a better place but wouldn't say he's happy with what he has accomplished so far.
text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had a conversation with his uncle before training camp in 2025. His uncle was asking about his nephew's journey to NFL stardom, when he became a Pro Bowl player while setting a Giants record with 109 receptions during his rookie season.

Nabers, the sixth overall pick out of LSU in 2024, told him how he didn't view his journey as all that hard. In fact, it came relatively easy for the wide receiver while compiling 1,204 yards and seven touchdowns despite playing with four quarterbacks in 2024. Nabers noted there were a lot of other players who had gone through "way harder things."

Little did he know what was coming.

Fast forward to three months later in Week 4 of the 2025 season against the Los Angeles Chargers, with Nabers lying on the MetLife Stadium turf reaching for his right knee. He had jumped to make a catch deep down the right sideline and knew immediately, in midair, that something was wrong.

The Giants' young playmaker tore the ACL and meniscus in his right knee.

This was the test he subconsciously knew was coming even if it was one he hadn't asked for.

On Nov. 1, 2026, Nabers is standing in the middle of the Giants' locker room seemingly fully back after four straight 100-yard receiving games, answering questions about the emotional challenge that came with the serious knee injury that cost him most of last season.

Nabers revealed to ESPN prior to the first-place Giants' matchup Thursday night with the Washington Commanders (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime) details about that private conversation with his uncle that left the wide receiver once upon a time thinking his journey wouldn't be that formidable.

"Kind of ... kind of just ... and then this happened," Nabers reminisced last week. "And I was like, OK, well, this is the challenge that I said I never had. It's an opportunity to get back from a challenge and see how I can come back off of it."

Nabers found out the physical and mental toll recovering from such a significant injury would entail ups and downs in the process, everything from lack of flexion in his knee to a second "cleanup" procedure to eliminate stiffness.

The original thought from the Giants was that he would be back in the spring. Then even the summer and training camp was in doubt.

"He had a slow comeback process just due to the severity of his injury," said Dr. Sharif "Reef" Tabbah, a physical therapist who worked with Nabers in Miami earlier this year.

Nabers tried hard to keep his faith, believing and telling himself everything was going to be fine when, in reality, he had no idea. The thoughts were bouncing like a ping pong ball off a wall, volleyed away but returning with a vengeance.

"He was definitely struggling. You could tell he was struggling with the process," said Giants coach John Harbaugh, who was hired in January. "He even told me he was never hurt before, how hard it was. I think every little up and down in the process would really affect him emotionally, mentally, whatever."

Nabers was going through an internal battle during a long and hard rehab. Through it all, he was trying to find himself. There were days when he was searching for answers but couldn't find them. He would have to figure out where and when they would come from. It wasn't going to be easy.

"I kind of lost myself in the process," Nabers said while opening up about his rehab for the first time.

NABERS' INJURY HISTORY prior to the Giants was not extensive. There was a shoulder injury that forced him to miss a couple of games at LSU his freshman season. He had some problems with his toe in New York, but nothing major. No long-term injuries or extended periods out of football.

This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place.

"Just my attitude," Nabers said of why he lost himself. "Everybody didn't know what my mindset was. Just at a loss for words. Didn't really have a lot of words to say. Didn't really have, I don't know, I kind of was empty. Just didn't know what the future holds, how I was going to respond, just with everything that was going on. Everybody just didn't know."

There were days when his knee swelled, when it was stiff and didn't bend. His progress, if it was outlined in a graph, might resemble the stock market during its most volatile month.

This sent Nabers into a tailspin. He was fighting himself.

"My mind was just all over the place. I didn't really understand and didn't really want to communicate well," he said. "Just didn't know how to communicate how I was feeling and how things were going because every day it was something new. ... So I just didn't know, I just didn't really see a process. I didn't really see progress from week to week."

Nabers said he didn't lean on anyone in particular, not even Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, one of his closest friends -- who also spent this past offseason combating an injury-plagued season. He was around Giants running back Cam Skattebo a bunch as they both rehabbed injuries -- Skattebo suffered an open fracture to his right leg in October of last year and still ultimately returned for the start of mandatory minicamp before Nabers. But Nabers kept to himself. He didn't feel like sharing.

"When he was in that deep place, I was in that deep place, too. We were both together," Skattebo said. "We were both in that same spot as not being able to say anything, not being able to express ourselves. ... He wasn't seeing the progress that he wanted but as he kept going and up until now, he's starting to feel that progress that's being made."

In a way, it was an extension of Nabers' nature. He is generally a quiet guy.

"When you go through an internal battle with yourself you start to figure out what you need better than other people telling you what you need when they don't know you," Nabers said. "... You start finding more about yourself that you didn't know yet. ... So I just went through it myself."

RECOVERY FROM A torn ACL can be a beast. Adding a full meniscus repair only adds to the difficulty.

It's why Nabers was still walking with crutches and wearing a brace in January, some two-plus months after the surgery was performed by Dallas Cowboys head team physician Daniel E. Cooper -- a renowned doctor known for recently operating on other NFL players such as Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers. Typically, full meniscus repair adds to the recovery timeline. It turned out to be the case for Nabers, who almost didn't play Week 1 roughly a year after his injury.

"His rehab protocol was a little bit slow," Tabbah said. "He had a lot of limitations still with mobility and strength and tolerance of functional exercises and things like that. So we were in that phase of ... tolerating different functional movement patterns and trying to get him ready to progress to that later stage."

Dr. Reef, as he is known, is a doctor of physical therapy and certified strength and conditioning specialist who founded Alkeme Sports RX in South Florida. He has worked with a long list of professional athletes, including Commanders wide receiver Stephon Diggs last year as he rehabbed from a torn ACL.

Dr. Reef worked with Nabers in Florida for most of February through May. He admitted it was a "challenging rehab case." But, along with new Giants trainer Adam Bennett, they together a plan that would be best for Nabers' healing. Together, they monitored the wide receiver's rehab, and early on in the process, Nabers needed the mental boost.

"I just try to give them reassurance and just let them know, 'Hey, this will pass. I know this is tough right now, but this is where you are today. It's not where you're going to be in months to come,'" Dr. Reef said. "I know this is your first rodeo when it comes to dealing with something like this, but it's not mine."

It was Dr. Reef's 15th season working with athletes. Diggs' ability to return to the field strong last season was a selling point Tabbah noted. He also kept reminding Nabers his process was different from everyone else's and warned against Nabers comparing himself to others because no injury is the same. Each comes with its own complexities.

It was when Nabers was back working with the Giants in the spring when significant strides were made. He had a second procedure in early spring, considered a cleanup to remove scar tissue and decrease stiffness.

"We had gone on the field, done a little bit of some footwork. We had done some bag work a little bit," Dr. Reef said. "And then every time we'd make some progress, he'd get a flare up and we'd go backwards. So that's when we eventually said, 'Hey, let's get this thing cleaned out.'"

Nabers then began making significant progress late in the spring/early in the summer working with rehabilitation and return-to-play coordinator Allison Boudtrou and the Giants' medical staff. He spent a good chunk of his summer getting well in New Jersey.

The end was in sight.

The Giants thought it was important for Nabers to get on the field this summer. They decided not to have him start on the physically unable to perform list. It was important for Nabers to do what he could to get over both the physical and mental humps.

Even when he wasn't able to do much physical movement in the spring, the Giants were managing his mind as much as his body. Wide receivers coach Chad Hall made him go through walk-throughs just to get his focus off the weight of rehab.

Nabers wanted to start by learning one position in the new offense. Hall and the Giants said no. They wanted to give him more to keep him occupied and ready. They were managing his mindset.

"Challenge him in different ways so he can focus more on [the football] stuff," Hall said.

That is where Nabers thrives -- playing football. It's where he wanted to be and the Giants were working to get him there.

NABERS WAS ON the field practicing at the start of this season's training camp. Considering where he was a few months earlier, it's hardly a surprise that he said his "soul came back to life," after practicing in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia. He was ready for the season opener against the Dallas Cowboys despite legitimate uncertainty about whether he would actually play.

Finally in his happy place. No longer lost. Still waiting for the breakthrough.

"I guess I'm still waiting for that moment," Nabers said.

Even though he looks good and the production is there, the star wide receiver believes there is still more progress to be made mentally and physically. Nabers was insistent the first few weeks of the 2026 season that he was "rusty." He was slipping coming out of routes and still learning to trust the right knee.

Then he had a stretch of four straight 100-yard games that ended Sunday in Week 9 at Philadelphia. He currently ranks 11th in the NFL with 648 receiving yards on 53 catches.

It seems Nabers, who took offense this week to Fox broadcaster Greg Olsen's comments about his body language, is back to his pre-injury form. But don't tell him that.

"Working on it," he said. "Working on it."

The biggest thing he has learned is patience. Nabers also still believes there's more to go physically. He feels he can get stronger and improve flexion in the knee. But there's likely always going to be a next level he's looking to reach.

The wide receiver is admittedly in a better place but wouldn't say he's happy with what he has accomplished so far.

In his mind, the comeback is not yet complete.

title: Jalen Hurts played through pain. Why do we keep celebrating it? - The Athletic
authors: Katrina Monton, Elise Devlin and Reuben Pinder
description:
Last month, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts sought treatment for a calf injury.
Hurts is now expected to miss the remainder of the season, though the team anticipates a full recovery.
In 2023, he continued competing through a knee injury, and the following season, he played with a broken finger.
What I keep coming back to is this: We assume pushing athletes beyond their limits produces excellence, but what if that approach is actually holding them back?
Once we knew Hurts was more seriously injured and had blood clots in both lungs, Robinson apologized for his comments.
text:
This story is part of Peak, The Athletic’s desk covering the mental side of sports. Sign up for Peak’s newsletter here.

Katrina Monton is an organizational psychologist and professor at Rutgers University. She also played water polo for Team Canada, winning a silver medal at the 2009 World Championships.

Last month, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts sought treatment for a calf injury. He practiced in the days following the injury and, before the Eagles’ next game in London, was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his leg. Doctors determined that he could safely compete, and so he did.

Further testing revealed a more serious condition: a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in both lungs. Hurts is now expected to miss the remainder of the season, though the team anticipates a full recovery.

In the past, Hurts has been admired for his willingness to push through injuries and adversity. In 2023, he continued competing through a knee injury, and the following season, he played with a broken finger. His ability to compete through pain has earned praise from coaches and teammates, with head coach Nick Sirianni saying Hurts “can play through anything,” and teammate Jordan Mailata describing him as a warrior.

As a former elite athlete and now an organizational psychologist, I see this as more than a single unfortunate incident; it’s a moment that invites us to think about how elite sport normalizes pain, rewards self-sacrifice and too often puts performance ahead of athletes’ health.

I’ve seen this mentality throughout professional sport, and I’ve experienced it myself.

When I made Canada’s national water polo team, I was 14. I then spent almost 15 years competing on the international stage. There was this idea that we were expected to show up ready to train, compete and put everything else on the backburner. It didn’t matter if we were injured, sick or had something going on in our personal lives.

We all knew how replaceable we were.

On the national team, I took pride in my ability to push through whatever was happening in my life. I wore that toughness as a badge of honor, and it became attached to my identity and how I understood myself.

It made me feel I had earned my place on the team.

Most of us who grew up in the 1990s and early 2000s were surrounded by slogans exhorting this mentality: No pain, no gain. No days off. Win at all costs.

So when I suffered a concussion near the end of my career, the pressure to quickly return didn’t need to come from anyone else. By then, years of competing in an environment that celebrated and rewarded toughness and pushing through pain had taught me to expect the same of myself.

We were less than four months away from the Olympic qualifier in 2016. I got hit in the face with the ball at very close range. I was so disoriented and dazed that I actually swam into our own net.

I went to the side of the pool and tried to shake it off. I remember telling our trainer: “I’m good, I’m good.” There was some pride in that response.

I finished training that morning and came back that evening for a scrimmage. It wasn’t until I finished weight training the next day that I felt so nauseous that I nearly vomited. Even then, I thought: Must have the flu!

Eventually, I returned to competition even though I was experiencing pretty frequent headaches.

It’s a very strange attitude to explain. It was like I wasn’t thinking about my own body and my own symptoms. It was just programmed in me.

Looking back, I can question that mentality in a way I wasn’t able to at the time. Now I think: I wonder what that recovery would have looked like if I hadn’t spent years absorbing those messages from coaches, teammates and a broader society that celebrated and rewarded pushing through pain.

I’ve since dedicated my career to understanding how these expectations can undermine the very excellence they try to achieve.

What I keep coming back to is this: We assume pushing athletes beyond their limits produces excellence, but what if that approach is actually holding them back? If we respected those limits instead of overriding them, could we unlock levels of performance we haven’t even begun to imagine?

In my own research with retired Olympic athletes, many participants described pressures very similar to what I experienced. They feared that disclosing an injury or expressing vulnerability could jeopardize their spot on the team. One athlete recalled seeking medical treatment outside her team’s healthcare system because she was afraid that revealing that injury might end her career. Other participants I interviewed talked about skipping MRIs and competing on broken bones.

The problem isn’t athletes who tough it out. It’s the culture of sport that makes speaking up and being honest about your injuries so costly.

We tend to celebrate winning at all costs, even if we may not realize we’re doing it. We treat pushing through pain as proof of commitment. And the stakes are so high. An injury can jeopardize playing time or a spot on the team, which can impact an athlete’s livelihood.

I read an article after Hurts was initially sidelined with the blood clot diagnosis. A former NFL player, Michael Robinson, suggested on NFL Network that Hurts was using his injury to distance himself from the Eagles’ struggling season, even encouraging viewers to compare a superficial blood clot with a “real” one.

Once we knew Hurts was more seriously injured and had blood clots in both lungs, Robinson apologized for his comments. But I think his initial reaction is revealing. It reinforces the belief that athletes are expected to push through pain, and when they can’t, their toughness, commitment and willingness to put their team first are called into question.

I’m not in the business of reducing or removing challenges. That’s why sports are so captivating and powerful. But teams and organizations can create better environments for athletes to have more open and honest conversations. We can do right by the athlete and right by the situation.

When I had my concussion, the conversations I remember having with doctors and coaches were almost entirely about what I needed to do to get back in the pool. There was little discussion about my long-term health, the potential consequences of returning too soon, or even what I wanted. The focus was on getting me back to competition. I still experience migraines today.

I’ve often wondered what it would have been like if we’d had a more open and honest conversation: I really want to play, and I really want to get back, but what does that look like? What should I be comfortable pushing through, and what shouldn’t I? What are the potential consequences for my health, not just now, but years down the road?

Through my work with Speed Skating Canada, which has won more Olympic medals than any other summer or winter Canadian sport, I received a front-row seat to these kinds of changes.

They wanted their athletes to be vocal. They said: We want people to be leaders, to be thinkers, to be pushing back and challenging us.

It’s a true collaboration when it’s done well. In subsequent research, athletes described feeling comfortable raising concerns, sharing doubts and telling coaches when something wasn’t working for them.

And they still won.

We should all be asking not only what athletes are willing to sacrifice for success but whether those sacrifices are necessary, what they cost and why we so rarely recognize the courage it takes to prioritize one’s health.

The next time we celebrate an athlete for being a warrior, we might also consider what we’re asking of the human being behind that performance.

text:
The San Francisco 49ers' convincing 38-17 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders came with a devastating cost. Rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton, who emerged as one of the defensive bright spots of the 2026 rookie class, suffered a season-ending broken ankle late in the fourth quarter on Sunday.

The injury halted what was otherwise a celebration for the NFC-leading 49ers (7-1). With Las Vegas facing fourth-and-long inside the final minutes, Halton went down awkwardly on a rush attempt. The scene turned somber immediately and players from both sidelines took a knee, and the entire 49ers roster cleared the sideline to surround the cart and support the visibly emotional rookie as he was transported off the field.

Head coach Kyle Shanahan confirmed postgame that Halton sustained a fractured ankle, shutting down his rookie campaign just as he was carving out a crucial role in San Francisco's interior rotation.

A Sensation in the Making: Halton's Stellar Rookie Campaign

Selected in the fourth round (No. 107 overall) out of Oklahoma, Halton wasted no time proving his explosiveness translated to the pro level. In pre-draft testing, his athletic profile jumped off the charts, and defensive line coach Kris Kocurek quickly integrated him into high-leverage situations.

Through his first eight NFL games, starting six, Halton was actively making game-changing plays in both phases:

Before going down on Sunday, Halton was creating havoc once again. On the snap immediately following a Brock Purdy interception in the third quarter, Halton tipped and nearly intercepted a Kirk Cousins pass at the line of scrimmage, setting up Fred Warner's fumble-forcing punch one play later.

Earlier in the year, Halton cemented his place on highlight reels with a scoop-and-score fumble recovery touchdown, showcasing rare quickness and lateral agility for a 292-pound interior defender.

What It Means for the 49ers' Defensive Line

Losing Halton is a significant blow to the 49ers' interior defensive depth, but the front office's proactive aggression ahead of the NFL trade deadline softens the impact.

Just days before Halton's injury, general manager John Lynch shipped a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to reacquire veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. While the move originally looked like an opportunity to build a dominant, fresh rotation between Buckner, Halton, and Kevin Givens, Halton's injury now thrusts Buckner into an indispensable, every-down role inside alongside Nick Bosa.

Halton will undergo surgery and turn his focus toward rehabilitation with an eye on returning at full strength for the 2027 season. For San Francisco, the challenge will be matching the sheer disruption, motor, and edge that their rookie tackle brought to the field every Sunday.

text:
Lucas Patrick is out Thursday night against the New York Giants. The Commanders’ final injury report also ruled out tight end Colson Yankoff, leaving Washington to start Nick Allegretti at center in place of Patrick.

Patrick entered concussion protocol during Sunday’s loss to the Rams, and rookie Matt Gulbin finished that game at center. Head coach Dan Quinn confirmed Tuesday that Allegretti will start against New York. Gulbin got the call Sunday because he had been taking the center reps while Allegretti worked at guard, a decision I wrote more about earlier this week. According to Washington's official website, the Giants blitz at the third-highest rate in the NFL. Allegretti will have to help set the protection against that defense with Jayden Daniels behind him.

Treylon Burks missed Wednesday’s practice with the foot injury that kept him out against the Rams, but he has no game designation. Quinn said the day off was planned after Burks got work Tuesday and that the receiver was expected to be ready Thursday. Washington did not practice Monday and held a walkthrough Tuesday, so those first two participation reports were estimates. Burks’ place on the active list will be confirmed with Thursday’s inactives.

Yankoff did not practice during the short week because of a knee injury. His absence reaches beyond the tight end rotation: Washington credited him with 185 special teams snaps this season. John Bates (shoulder) was full all three days, and Chig Okonkwo (hip) was full Tuesday and Wednesday. Neither has a game designation.

Daniels (left elbow) and Gulbin (knee) practiced fully throughout the week. Shy Tuttle (shoulder) was full Tuesday and Wednesday, while Amik Robertson (ankle) also finished without a game designation.

New York listed linebacker Malik Harrison (groin) as questionable after he was limited all week. Quarterback J.J. McCarthy (hip) and running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) finished without game designations, as did Abdul Carter (knee/back), who was listed as full Wednesday after two limited days.

title: Packers-Vikings Wednesday Injury Report: Huge List Filled With Big Names
description:

Well, he would have been limited participation, as well, with an ankle injury.
Kicker Trey Smack (right calf) and receiver Savion Williams (groin) were listed as limited participation, as well.
Skyy Moore Designated for Return Receiver Skyy Moore was designated for return after missing the last four games with an ankle injury.
Vikings Injury Update The big news in Minnesota – other than trading for Kirk Cousins – is that star linebacker Blake Cashman is in the concussion protocol.
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers kicked off their biggest week of the season with their longest injury report of the year.

Officially, the Packers did not practice on Wednesday as they get ready for Sunday’s showdown against the Minnesota Vikings. If they would have, five starters would not have practiced and a total of 16 players were dealing with one issue or another.

Nickel Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), running back Josh Jacobs (finger), center Sean Rhyan (ankle), edge Lukas Van Ness (back) and tight end Josh Whyle (concussion) would not have practiced.

Rhyan was injured during the opening series at Detroit. So, he missed most of that game and then the next two games. Coach Matt LaFleur said Rhyan could “potentially” return this week, but that he would not have practiced on Wednesday might not be a good sign for Sunday.

That means John Williams could be in line for his third career start – and his first against the most aggressive defense in the league.

“Banked reps and experience, you can't beat that,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “If we were on a away game, it would be even more critical because sometimes John having his head between his legs, those are the guys that got to communicate a lot of looks. So, it'll be good for John to be at home, he'll be able to see everything and make all those calls.”

Franklin has missed the last three games due to an injury sustained at practice before the Detroit game.

Finally, Van Ness was a noteworthy addition. He played 32 of the 63 snaps against New England and contributed one tackle. He leads the team with 4.5 sacks.

More Starters Were Limited

The questions on the offensive line run deeper than center. Left guard Aaron Banks (knee/hip) would have been limited participation, a continuation of a season filled with injuries. He’s played only 137 snaps. Of his three starts, he was unable to go the distance against the Jets in Week 2 or the Patriots last week.

When Banks was knocked out of the New England game, Kevin Zeitler made his Packers debut. Well, he would have been limited participation, as well, with an ankle injury.

Linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper, who played only two defensive snaps vs. the Patriots due to a pregame chest injury, would have been limited due to illness; the chest is not mentioned on the injury report.

Kicker Trey Smack (right calf) and receiver Savion Williams (groin) were listed as limited participation, as well.

One starter not on the injury report is Love. He was knocked to the turf at one point last week and got up flexing his left hand.

“It was just one of those weird ones where it just get hits, so it’s fine,” he said.

Skyy Moore Designated for Return

Receiver Skyy Moore was designated for return after missing the last four games with an ankle injury. He is averaging 16.0 yards per punt return, highlighted by a 63-yarder against the Jets, and 27.5 yards per kickoff return. Both figures lead the team.

On offense, he caught seven passes for only 35 yards.

“He's been such a great returner for us,” Love said. “It'll definitely be huge to get him back and I'm grateful that we're able to get him back this week.”

Running back Chris Brooks (ankle) and edge Micah Parsons (knee/illness), who are entering their second week of practice after being designated for return, would have been limited. Brooks would be a big addition against the Vikings’ blitzing defense.

Vikings Injury Update

The big news in Minnesota – other than trading for Kirk Cousins – is that star linebacker Blake Cashman is in the concussion protocol. That’s never good news for any team or player, but that’s especially noteworthy considering the Vikings are coming off a Monday night game, so Cashman will have a day less to recover.

“He had the stinger evaluation going on and then did end up taking a hit, or more than likely giving a hit, later on in that game. He is currently in the concussion protocol,” Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell told reporters. “Obviously, short week. He's doing really, really well, but I'll keep you guys posted on him as we go through the week.”

Cashman leads the Vikings with 76 tackles, including seven tackles and two tackles for losses in Week 1. He’s in the top three on the team with 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for losses, 10 quarterback hits and seven passes defensed. Cashman is 10th in the league in tackles. From that group, nobody has more sacks, tackles for losses, quarterback hits or pass breakups.

In fact, no player with even 50 tackles has 10 quarterback hits. Cashman and Tampa Bay’s Josiah Trotter (70 tackles) are the only players with 60-plus tackles and seven PBUs. He is an elite player.

“Cash is an important part of our defense,” defensive coordinator Brian Flores said last season. “He’s a big part of what we do defensively from a communication standpoint, just an athleticism, football acumen. Getting other guys in the right positions, leadership. He does a great job.”

Packers Wednesday Injury Report

Did not participate: S Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), LB Zaire Franklin (shin), RB Josh Jacobs (finger), C Sean Rhyan (ankle), edge Lukas Van Ness (back), TE Josh Whyle (concussion).

Limited participation: LG Aaron Banks (knee/hip), RB Chris Brooks (ankle), G/T Travis Glover (knee), LB Ty’Ron Hopper (illness), WR Skyy Moore (ankle), edge Micah Parsons (knee/illness), K Trey Smack (right calf), WR Savion Williams (groin), G Kevin Zeitler (ankle).

Full participation: WR Bo Melton (gameday concussion evaluation).

Note: Brooks, Moore and Parsons have been designated to return and are within their 21-day practice window.

Vikings Wednesday Injury Report

Did not participate: LB Blake Cashman (concussion), TE T.J. Hockenson (wrist/chest), DL Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins (ankle), WR Jauan Jennings (calf), QB Kyler Murray (hamstring), OLB Kyle Van Noy (calf).

Limited participation: S Jay Ward (knee), QB Carson Wentz (ankle).

Full participation: S Theo Jackson (quad).

text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- The Miami Dolphins are hopeful quarterback Malik Willis will return this season after his mandated minimum four-game stay on injured reserve, coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday, and Willis is expected to remain the team's starter upon his return.

Hafley said Willis' MRI showed his groin injury had progressed to his core and the Dolphins' medical team believed he "needed the rest." Willis will seek a second opinion on his injury this week to decide whether or not to undergo surgery, but the Dolphins still see him as their starter, regardless of when he returns.

"Our hope is that he'll be back after his four weeks, which in time, if healthy, he'll return," Hafley said. "But he will be the starter when healthy, when he does return. And again, you look back at Malik and you watch him in that last game and you could see it. He couldn't quite move the way he had done early in the year and he was gritting through it and he was toughing through it. He made some plays with his feet in that game to keep plays alive.

"But we want him to be healthy so he can play at a high level without risking further injury."

Willis received treatment on his groin in each of the past two weeks. It didn't limit his practice participation, but he was noticeably hobbled in last week's loss to the Detroit Lions and was held to single-digit rushing yards for the second game in a row.

With Willis sidelined, second-year quarterback Kyle McCord will get his first career start Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts.

The Dolphins traded for McCord from the Green Bay Packers in August after the former sixth-round pick led the NFL in passing touchdowns this preseason. Though McCord has primarily run the Dolphins' scout team at practice since his arrival, Hafley said McCord's preseason tape showed desirable traits.

"He's got a strong arm, stronger than you think. He sees it well. The ball comes out fast," Hafley said. "He's decisive. He's aggressive. ... Again, he does not have experience in this league and this league is very different, but he does have experience. He has played in a lot of games, but from when I watched him, he's thrown a lot of passes and he does have arm talent and the ball comes out quickly and it'll be interesting to see."

The Philadelphia Eagles took McCord in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL draft, after he threw for an FBS-leading 4,779 yards at Syracuse as a senior. He also spent three seasons at Ohio State, going 11-1 as a starter in 2023.

McCord said it is his big-game experience in college that gives him confidence heading into the biggest week of his NFL career to date.

"It's a blessing, but I think once you get the first play, put on the helmet and get going, I think it'll feel just like football," McCord said of his opportunity. "And I feel like ... that's something that having played those big college games, I think you've been in those moments before my first time playing in a big game. I feel like that's where I'm drawing a lot of confidence from."

McCord said that despite his brief time in Miami, he has a full grasp of the playbook and can run "anything [offensive coordinator] Bobby [Slowik] wants to call." According to teammates, he has already shown that grasp at practice this week.

Right tackle Austin Jackson said McCord wasn't afraid to correct his teammates at Wednesday's practice, specifically when they weren't lined up appropriately.

"I would say he seemed pretty confident today in the huddle, calling the huddle, pretty confident calling the plays out," Jackson said. "There's a couple times the formation was wrong and he actually spotted it out beforehand, which is good. That's something that is big for a quarterback ... the confidence there is the main thing really, at the end of the day, that gets [a quarterback] through it."

Left tackle Patrick Paul said McCord has a "moxie" to him that he's excited for people to see Sunday and said he wasn't surprised by his practice habits "because he's a smart player."

Paul also said Miami's offensive line has a responsibility to ensure McCord remains comfortable during his first start.

"As the O-line, you have to make him feel comfortable," Paul said. "So that's setting a firm pocket and then just off the field, getting with him, talking with him, making sure he's confident, and then just praising him when you can -- just letting him know that you're there and supporting him."

text:
Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce remains in rehab for a heel injury with no set timeline for his return.

Pierce reaggravated the injury in Week 2 after undergoing surgery in late March.

The Colts recently traded their top two healthy receivers, Josh Downs and Keenan Allen.

Despite playing only five quarters, Pierce is still among the team's top three wideouts in catches and yards.

INDIANAPOLIS – Colts lead wide receiver Alec Pierce remains in rehab seven weeks after reaggravating his surgically repaired left heel early in the Colts’ Week 2 road loss to the Chiefs, Colts head coach Shane Steichen said Wednesday. Steichen declined to give a timeline on a possible return for Pierce or commit to the return of the team’s top receiver at all.

Pierce missed nearly all of the Colts’ offseason workout programs after undergoing surgery on the foot in late-March. Doctors at the time told Pierce to expect a four-to-six-month rehab process and Pierce returned to practice Aug. 27, just longer than two weeks before the team’s first game. He played a reduced number of snaps in Week 1 – 32 of 54 – but was set to play near a normal role in a Sunday Night Football contest in Week 2 in Kansas City before going down a quarter into the contest while running a route.

The fifth-year receiver was carted back to the locker room for imaging, and he was seen using crutches to exit the building following the team’s overtime loss. The Colts then placed Pierce on injured reserve, meaning he would miss at least the team’s next four games but be eligible to return as soon as Week 7 in Minnesota. Just days before that opportunity, Pierce was seen by reporters in the press box at the team’s Week 6 game at Lucas Oil Stadium in a walking boot.

“He’s still in the rehab process, and I’m not going to put a timetable on his return,” Steichen said Wednesday when asked whether it was still realistic for Pierce to return before the end of the season.

Currently on a five-game losing streak, the Colts sit 2-7 heading into a winnable Week 10 home matchup against the Dolphins, and Indianapolis is staring at one of the NFL’s easiest schedules over the rest of the season – only three of its final eight games are against teams in the playoff picture.

Tuesday, the Colts dealr the team’s top two healthy receivers in Josh Downs (to Kansas City) and Keenan Allen (to San Francisco). On Sunday, the team is slated to roll out Anthony Gould, Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Deion Burks and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine as its options at receiver with Pierce still on IR – a group that has combined for 27 catches for 375 receiving yards this season.

Though Pierce has only played five quarters and 49 total offensive snaps this year, he still ranks top 3 on the team among rostered wideouts in catches (five) and receiving yards (72).

The Colts did open the 21-day practice window Wednesday for veteran edge rusher Arden Key, who has missed the Colts' last five games with a hamstring injury he suffered during the team’s Week 4 game in London. Key logged his first practice since suffering the injury on Wednesday and was a full participant.

text:
The dust has finally settled after a wild few weeks leading up to the trade deadline, with lots of big names in new places.

Unfortunately, lots of big names will be nowhere to be found -- at least not on the field -- as we enter Week 10. There were several injuries to key players in Week 9, none bigger than Puka Nacua suffering a significant knee injury. Though the Rams have not officially put the superstar wide receiver on IR, he is facing a multi-week absence as the Rams' snakebitten season continues. Other notable names going down with injury Sunday included Rhamondre Stevenson, Josh Jacobs, Malik Willis, Jaylen Waddle, Luther Burden III, Riley Moss and Antoine Winfield Jr.

Quarterbacks Patrick Mahomes (elbow) and Justin Herbert (finger/hand) appear to have avoided major injury, but their respective statuses are worth monitoring going forward, too. Herbert will have one extra day to heal as the Chargers play on Monday night against the Ravens.

Here's the initial injury report for each team playing on Sunday in Week 10, as well as the final injury report for the Giants-Commanders "Thursday Night Football" matchup.

Odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook

Commanders at Giants (-2.5)

Commanders: C Lucas Patrick (concussion), TE Colson Yankoff (knee) OUT

Giants: LB Malik Harrison (groin) QUESTIONABLE

Washington will be down one starter in Patrick; Nick Allegretti figures to slot in there. Otherwise, it's a mostly clean injury report, with the return of Treylon Burks a potential boost for the downfield passing game. He missed Week 9 with a foot injury.

The Giants have one of their cleanest injury reports of the year. Notably, running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) will be back after missing Week 9 with a hamstring injury, and coach John Harbaugh said he will be "full go" in this NFC East meeting.

Patriots at Lions (-2.5) in Munich

New England ruled out offensive lineman Ben Brown (knee), cornerback Carlton Davis III (knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness), and all three did not participate in Wednesday's practice. Also not participating were tight end Cameron Latu (back), offensive lineman Walter Rouse (concussion), safety Brenden Schooler (hamstring) and running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee). Stevenson is expected to miss at least this week with the injury he suffered Sunday. Wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee), safety Kevin Byard III (chest), fullback Reggie Gilliam (knee), tight end Hunter Henry (foot), tackle Morgan Moses (foot), offensive lineman Greg Van Roten (hamstring) and cornerback Charles Woods (hamstring) were all limited. Brown hasn't played since Week 7 and has played in just three contests this year.

Center Cade Mays (ankle), cornerback D.J. Reed (hip) and running back Sione Vaki (ankle) did not practice Wednesday; Mays and Reed are considered long shots to play. Defensive back Brian Branch (hip), quarterback Jared Goff (chest), safety Kerby Joseph (knee) and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib) were all limited.

Texans (-4.5) at Browns

Four Texans players did not practice Wednesday: linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair (groin/personal), tight end Brevin Jordan (finger/foot), running back David Montgomery (groin) and offensive lineman Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder). Montgomery has not played since suffering the injury in Week 5. Wide receiver Tank Dell (hand/shoulder), running back Woody Marks (knee), safety Reed Blankenship (concussion/hand), wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring), cornerback Jaylin Smith (hamstring), linebacker Jake Hummel (groin) and offensive lineman Wyatt Teller (illness) were all limited for Houston in ahead of a crucial matchup in the AFC playoff race.

Wide receiver Denzel Boston (toe), fullback Michael Burton (calf), safety Ronnie Hickman (concussion) and center Elgton Jenkins (knee) all did not practice for the Browns on Wednesday. Boston has played through a couple of injuries this year, and Jenkins has played through his knee ailment, too. Tackle Austin Barber (calf), defensive tackle Maliek Collins (elbow), tight end Harold Fannin Jr. (groin), tackle Tytus Howard (knee), linebacker Carson Schwesinger (wrist/ankle), cornerback Denzel Ward (cornerback) and linebacker Quincy Williams (hamstring) were all limited. Deshaun Watson, who cleared concussion protocol last week but did not play, was not on the injury report and will start this weekend. Shedeur Sanders played all of Cleveland's Week 9 loss to the Saints.

Chiefs (-3.5) at Falcons

The Chiefs listed two players as "DNP" on Wednesday: offensive lineman Jaylon Moore (ankle) and defensive lineman Peter Woods (neck), but by far the biggest news was Patrick Mahomes (elbow) being able to practice fully. He suffered what looked like a potentially serious elbow injury against the Jets but was able to return to the game. Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (knee) was limited.

The Falcons were without wide receiver Zachariah Branch (hamstring), linebacker Josh Woods (ankle) and EDGE James Pearce Jr. (back). Branch missed last week's contest while Pearce, in his first game back from suspension, logged just 15 snaps after the back issue flared up late in the week. Defensive lineman Gervon Dexter St. (illness) and EDGE Za'Darius Smith (rest) also did not practice Wednesday. Linebacker Divine Deablo (forearm) was limited. He played with his arm wrapped in Week 9.

Panthers at Saints (-2.5)

The Panthers got a host of players back to practice Wednesday, which was really a walkthrough: EDGE Jaelan Phillips (hamstring), guard Damien Lewis (knee) and cornerback Will Lee III (hamstring) were all full participants. Phillips has missed the last three games, Lewis the last two and Lee the most recent one. Furthermore, cornerback Mike Jackson (groin), running back Jonathan Brooks (groin and wide receiver Xavier Legette (knee) were full participants after having their 21-day practice windows opened coming off IR. Linebacker Bobby Okereke (foot) and running back Chuba Hubbard (rest) did not participate.

The biggest returnee -- at least to practice -- for the Saints is running back Travis Etienne Jr., who remains on IR. He was limited with a hamstring injury. Running backs CJ Donaldson (shoulder). Alvin Kamara (rest/back) and center Erik McCoy (biceps) did not practice, and coach Kellen Moore said Cesar Ruiz will start at center this week. Tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. (ankle), guard David Edwards (knee), cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. (shin), tight end Noah Fant (back) and defensive lineman Christen Miller (knee) joined Etienne in the "limited" category.

Vikings at Packers (-3)

After playing on "Monday Night Football," the Vikings did not practice Wednesday, so their injury report reflects an estimate of participation. Linebacker Blake Cashman (concussion), tight end T.J. Hockenson (wrist/chest), defensive lineman Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins (ankle), wide receiver Jauan Jennings (calf), quarterback Kyler Murray (hamstring) and EDGE Kyle Van Noy (calf) were all listed as non-participants, while quarterback Carson Wentz (ankle) and safety Jay Ward (knee) were listed as limited. Coach Kevin O'Connell was hopeful Wentz would be able to back up newly acquired Kirk Cousins against Green Bay.

The Packers, meanwhile, reported that safety Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), offensive lineman Sean Rhyan (ankle), EDGE Lukas Van Ness (back) and tight end Josh Whyle (concussion) did not participate. Green Bay only held a jog-through, so the reports are an estimate. Guard Aaron Banks (knee/hip), running back Chris Brooks (ankle), offensive lineman Travis Glover (knee), linebacker Ty'Ron Hopper (illness), wide receiver Skyy Moore (ankle), EDGE Micah Parsons (knee/illness), kicker Trey Smack (calf), wide receiver Savion Williams (groin) and guard Kevin Zeitler (ankle) did not participate. Parsons remains on the PUP list, while Moore and Brooks are in their 21-day practice window.

Bills (-8.5) at Jets

The Bills, who played Monday night, only conducted a walk-through on Wednesday. Offensive lineman Alec Anderson (ankle), cornerback Christian Benford (wrist), tackle Spencer Brown (ankle), tackle Dion Dawkins (rib), tight end Dalton Kincaid (ankle) and center Connor McGovern (neck) were all limited. Anderson and Dawkins both missed Monday's win over the Vikings.

In their estimation, the Jets listed defensive lineman Harrison Phillips (ankle) and linebacker Trevin Wallace (groin) as "did not practice" Wednesday. Wide receivers Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle) and Garrett Wilson (concussion), EDGE Joseph Ossai (ankle), cornerback Nahshon Wright (back) and safety VJ Payne (knee) were all estimated to be limited. Wilson, the team's top wide receiver, did not play last week.

Jaguars (-10.5) at Titans

The Jaguars' big trade deadline additions -- safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis -- did not participate Wednesday, with "rest" listed as the reason for both. Also not practicing were wide receiver Jakobi Meyers (ankle), running back Bhayshul Tuten (ankle/foot) and defensive end Travon Walker (rib). Meyers, Tuten and Walker all played through said injuries last week. Offensive linemen Ezra Cleveland (knee/ankle) and Robert Hainsey (concussion), safety Antonio Johnson (ankle), running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. (hand) and linebacker Brason Combs (shoulder) were limited.

The Titans had five players -- linebackers Cody Barton (concussion) and Anthony Hill Jr. (neck), guard Peter Skoronski (hamstring), running back Tyjae Spears (knee) and wide receiver Carnell Tate (shoulder) listed as not participating. Tate and Spears both missed the Titans' last game, back in Week 8 before the team's bye, too.

Dolphins at Colts (-3.5)

Center Aaron Brewer (concussion) and tight end Will Kacmarek (quad/knee) were the only two Dolphins players not participating Wednesday. Long snapper Tucker Addington (shoulder), cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. (knee), wide receiver Chris Bell (knee) and EDGE Malik Herring (neck) were all limited. The team placed quarterback Malik Willis and defensive tackle Zach Sieler on IR on Tuesday, with Sieler's injury season-ending.

The Colts said tight end Mo Alie-Cox (groin), linebacker Jaylon Carlies (neck), linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee), safety AJ Haulcy (ankle), long snapper Luke Rhodes (hamstring), tackle Jalen Travis and cornerback Charvarius Ward (rest) did not practice. Running back Jonathan Taylor (rest) and defensive tackle Jerry Tillery (calf) were limited.

Rams (-9.5) at Cardinals

The Rams were without wide receiver Puka Nacua (knee/toe), cornerback Trent McDuffie (back), tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring), offensive lineman Steve Avila (hamstring) and safety Kam Curl (toe) at practice Wednesday. as has been the case all year, the star-studded group is quite banged up, though Sean McVay was optimistic McDuffie would return after missing Week 9. Tight end Davis Allen (oblique), long snapper Joe Cardona (ankle), defensive lineman Myles Garrett (knee) and tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs) were limited.

For the Cardinals, safety Budda Baker (rest), center Hjalte Froholdt (concussion), guard Jon Gaines II (ankle), defensive lineman Roy Loyez (toe/ankle), offensive lineman Isaac Seumalo (rest), EDGE Josh Sweat (rest) and linebacker Mack Wilson Sr. (rest/knee/ankle) did not participate. Running back Bam Knight (concussion), tight end Hunter Long (knee), cornerback Max Melton (knee/hand), defensive linemen Dante Stills (shoulder) and Zach Carter (knee), tackle Jayden Williams (knee) and safety Andrew Wingard (groin) were limited.

Seahawks (-6.5) at Raiders

The Seahawks released a lengthy Wednesday injury report that featured seven "DNP" designations. The biggest one is that Sam Darnold (ribs, quad) remains out, and the team will start Drew Lock (elbow, oblique) in Week 10, even though he was listed as limited. Joining Darnold in not participating were tackle Charles Cross (ankle), guard Quenton Nelson (knee), defensive tackles Brandon Pili (back) and Jarran Reed (personal), wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba (rest) and defensive end Leonard Williams (stinger). Along with Lock, guard Anthony Bradford (knee), EDGE Derick Hall (back), EDGE Uchenna Nwosu (ankle), linebacker Patrick O'Connell (toe) and EDGE Connor O'Toole (foot) were limited.

Every active Raiders player participated at least somewhat in the team's Wednesday practice. Defensive tackles Thomas Booker (ankle) and Foley Fotukasi (shoulder/back) were limited, as was guard Trey Zuhn III (concussion).

49ers (-4.5) at Cowboys

Wide receiver Mike Evans (Achilles), cornerback Renardo Greene (back), linebacker Dre Greenlaw (rest), cornerback Deommodore Lenoir (foot), running back Christian McCaffrey (rest) and tackle Trent Williams (rest) did not participate in 49ers practice Wednesday. Safety Siran Neal (knee, foot), cornerback Upton Stout (shoulder, neck), wide receiver Deebo Samuel (hamstring) and defensive tackle C.J. West (knee) were all limited. West had his practice window opened.

For the Cowboys, EDGE Donovan Ezeiruaku (ankle), tight end Jake Ferguson (knee/ankle), running back Tyler Goodson (ankle/knee), safety Malik Hooker (personal), defensive back P.J. Locke (concussion), EDGE Von Miller (rest), wide receiver Jonathan Mingo (ankle) and cornerback Joey Porter Jr. (ankle) did not practice. Ferguson and Goodson will miss extended periods, and Porter missed last week. Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown (hamstring/back), wide receiver George Pickens (hamstring) and wide receiver KaVontae Turpin (ribs) were limited. Overshown and Pickens missed last week, and Turpin has not played since mid-October.

Steelers at Bengals (-3.5)

Tight end Darnell Washington (rest), EDGE T.J. Watt (rest) and defensive tackle Cameron Heyward (rest) were the only Steelers who did not participate Wednesday. Safety DeShon Elliott (ankle) and defensive tackle Derrick Harmon (foot) were both limited; Harmon is currently designated to return from injured reserve and has not played since Week 4.

text:
ALLEN PARK — The Detroit Lions are expecting to get at least one player back for their game against the New England Patriots at Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, on Sunday, Nov. 15.

Lions coach Dan Campbell said Wednesday, Nov. 11, that DJ Wonnum (concussion) has cleared the first two obstacles necessary to return to practice and "should be good to go" against New England "as long as he gets through practice."

Wonnum suffered his injury against the Minnesota Vikings on Nov. 1 when he had a head-to-head collision with safety Brian Branch during a tackle of receiver Justin Jefferson. He missed last week's game against the Miami Dolphins.

As for cornerback D.J. Reed (hip) and center Cade Mays (ankle), Campbell said both players have a "way, way, way outside shot" of playing against New England and likely won't practice on Wednesday.

Reed and Mays were both injured in the Vikings game as well. Reed suffered a hip injury on a pass breakup in the fourth quarter and Mays suffered an ankle injury in the second quarter.

The good news for Detroit is that it has gotten solid play from its backup center. Juice Scruggs filled in admirably as Mays missed the season's first five games with a wrist injury and stepped right back in for a 19-9 win over the Dolphins.

With Reed out of the lineup, the Lions will continue relying on a rotation of Rock Ya-Sin, Roger McCreary, Ennis Rakestraw and Khalil Dorsey.

text:
The Steelers began their preparation for Sunday night's game against the Cincinnati Bengals, a key AFC North matchup with first place in the division on the line once again.

With the Steelers coming off the bye week, it was an opportunity for several players to get healthy, with multiple players eligible to return to practice this week.

Defensive tackle Derrick Harmon returned to practice today but remains on the Reserve/Injured List.

The Steelers have a 21-day window to either activate Harmon or he remains on the Reserve/Injured List for the remainder of the season. He was placed on the Reserve/Injured List on October 10.

Harmon, the Steelers No. 1 pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, appeared in four games this year, with one start, before he was placed on the Reserve/Injured List. He has 12 tackles this season, including three solo stops and a tackle for a loss. He also has one and a half sacks and a forced fumble.

In two seasons, Harmon has appeared in 16 games, with nine starts. He is credited with 39 tackles, including 14 solo tackles, as well as two tackles for a loss. He also has four and a half sacks, a pass defense and a forced fumble.

Receiver Michael Pittman Jr. is also eligible to return but hasn't yet. Pittman said last week he would like to return 'sooner rather than later' and McCarthy sees the progress he is making.

"I think Michael is getting close," said McCarthy on Monday. "I know his workout, I'm going to say Friday, was something that hopefully we can do more.

"We just want to get our guys, get them healthy. We're going to be obviously healthier than we've been in a while. So, it will be good to see really what Wednesday gives us as far as who we think is going to be ready for Cincinnati."

In addition, receiver Roman Wilson is eligible to come off the Reserve/Injured List following the Bengals game. Whether he returns to practice immediately is yet to be seen, but having everyone available would be a benefit to the offense.

"I think it will help all of them for sure," said offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio. "I think any time you can get your full group of guys back, it certainly eliminates the stress that other guys have to do to pick up the load."

With the situation the Steelers have dealt with at receiver over the last month with injuries, rookie Germie Bernard has become a go-to guy for quarterback Aaron Rodgers.

Bernard, who has started four games, has 32 receptions for 284 yards, an 8.9-yard average, and one touchdown.

"He's just getting more comfortable," said offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio. "You see the trust growing between them. He's really good with the ball in his hands, the run after the catch. It's a great job by Aaron getting him the ball, and he got us down to the one-yard line (against Cleveland), and then we clocked it.

"That was a great check, and guys are blocking downfield for him, (Pat Freiermuth) and DK (Metcalf), and Germ made it come to life. I think that's his strength. You saw it on the bubble early in the game in the run solution. He's always going forward. He's a tough tackle. He's got good explosion.

"I think the more he plays, the more trust, I think the more you'll see of it."

While the secondary is trending toward being a healthy group again, two players who have handled the next man up mentality through the first half of the season have been rookies Daylen Everett and Robert Spears-Jennings.

"They work really hard, and we hold them to a certain standard in terms of it doesn't matter, it's next man up when they get in the game, and those guys work really hard," said defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. "I enjoy seeing them play football. They're good football players.

"Both are physical. Both have a knack for getting to the ball. Then they work really hard, and they don't have a lot of repeat mistakes. I can't speak for the vets, but that's how they're earning the trust of the vets. Not a lot of repeat mistakes, they work hard, and they're a joy to be around."

text:
HOUSTON - Houston Texans QB C.J. Stroud has been named AFC Offensive Player of the Week, the NFL announced today.

In Week 9, Stroud earned a 125.5 passer rating while completing 21-of-35 (60.0%) passes for 384 yards and five touchdowns in a 44-22 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. The Texans opened the game on an eight-play, 73-yard drive, where Stroud completed five-of-five passes for 53 yards and a touchdown.

Stroud's five passing touchdowns tied his career high and marked the second time in his career that he has thrown for 350 yards while passing for five touchdowns, and his first since Nov. 5, 2023, versus Tampa Bay. His 384 passing yards and five touchdowns led the NFL in both categories in Week 9, and he recorded the third highest passer rating (125.5) in the NFL in Week 9. Stroud helped lead the Texans offense to the highest point total in the AFC in Week 9 (44), while being the only AFC quarterback to throw for over 300 passing yards. The Texans 44 points was tied for the most in franchise in a road game.

On the year, Stroud has completed 181-of-282 (64.2%) passes for 2,251 yards, 16 touchdowns and a passer rating of 104.8. Stroud leads the AFC in touchdown to interception ratio (8.0), is tied for first in completions of at least 20 yards (32), ranks second in passing yards per game (281.4) and ranks third in passer rating.

This marks the former Offensive Rookie of the Year's fifth AFC Offensive Player of the Week honor of his career. Stroud is the first player to win the AFC Offensive Player of the Week Award multiple times this season, and the first to do so since Josh Allen in 2025 (Week 1, Week 11 and Week 14).
